For this reason, the ālayavijñāna possesses various characteristics such as momentariness and so forth; that is to say, because it is subject to momentary destruction, because it co-exists with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), and because it continues to function throughout the cycle of birth and death until the arising of the path of antidotes; because it is determinately the cause of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so on; and because meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable formations depend upon conditions to ripen within the fortunate and unfortunate realms.
Because the ālayavijñāna is associated with such functions as these, it is able to receive perfuming; this must be established.
It is not consistent with reason that the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñānas) should [receive perfuming].
The six consciousnesses do not combine because the various consciousnesses are in constant flux.

Regarding their three distinct and contradictory characteristics: each consciousness arises based on its own respective support, takes its own respective object, and performs its own respective mental attention.
Furthermore, there is another meaning:
namely, that the various consciousnesses possess distinct characteristics.
The Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that a preceding moment of consciousness impregnates a subsequent moment.
To preclude this interpretation, the treatise states:
"Two moments do not coexist; there is no principle by which two moments could arise simultaneously."
If they arise and perish together, then perfuming can indeed be established.

If it is argued that although they do not conjoin, they can nevertheless perfume one another because the consciousnesses produced are of a similar nature, then by this same principle, other births would also necessarily be so.

It would follow that those with distinct characteristics should also be subject to this; for instance, since the various faculties such as the eye all share the characteristic of being translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*), they should be able to mutually perfume one another.
One should state it thus:
because the translucent matter of the eye-faculty and the translucent matter of the ear-faculty belong to the same category, those various translucent matters should mutually perfume one another.

Although pure matter is of the same nature, its locations are distinct; since it is not said that they mutually perfuse one another, how could consciousnesses—which, though of the same category—mutually perfume one another?
As it has been stated, there are two kinds of seeds, namely external and internal, both of which possess productive causes (*janakahetu*) and projecting causes (*ākṣepakahetu*).
Regarding external seeds as the cause of production, this extends until the fruit ripens.
Regarding internal seeds as the cause of production, this extends until the end of life.
Regarding external seeds as the projecting cause, this refers to those that have ripened but have not yet been sown.
Regarding internal seeds as projecting causes (*ākṣepa-hetu*), the corpse remains for a long duration after death due to this projecting cause.

If these two types of seeds were merely generative causes (*janana-hetu*), they would perish immediately upon being separated from their [projecting] cause; thus, there would be no possibility of them persisting through a long-term continuity.
If it is argued that because moments are transmitted and successively transformed, the preceding moment serves as the cause for the subsequent moment, then there would be no time of cessation;
yet since there is cessation, one should know that there must necessarily be an inducing cause.
Regarding these two seeds as the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*), it is, for example, like drawing a bow as the cause for an arrow to travel a great distance.
The treatise says:
These internal seeds are not analogous to external seeds; therefore, another verse is spoken:
External seeds lack perfuming; internal seeds are not so.
If hearing and the like lacked perfuming, the arising of their fruit would be illogical.
There would be the faults of contradiction regarding what has been done and what has not been done, and regarding loss and gain.
The external seeds take the internal as their condition, and they arise because of internal permeation (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are the experiencers with respect to all bodies and realms of existence (*gati*).
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "all bodies and realms therein are the experiencers," this means that within those [realms], they arise as experiencers.
Because they exist within the state of experiencing, they are called "experiencers."
This meaning is demonstrated by the *Madhyāntavibhāga-āgama*.
The treatise says:
"As stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*."
The first is the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition;
the second is the consciousness of experience, which is supported by all mental factors and discerns this experience.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, these two consciousnesses act as cause and effect for one another.
This is stated in the *āgama*, specifically in a verse from the *Abhidharma-sūtra*.
The treatise says:
These two types of consciousness also serve as mutual conditions for one another, as stated in a verse from the Abhidharma-sūtra:
"All phenomena abide dependent on consciousness, And consciousness likewise abides dependent on phenomena;
Each serves as the cause for the other, And they are likewise always mutually the result."
The commentary states:
Regarding their being mutual causes for one another, the ālayavijñāna is at all times the cause for the arising of all dharmas.
Furthermore, regarding their being constant mutual effects: if the ālayavijñāna is the cause, then all dharmas are the effect; if all dharmas are the cause, then the ālayavijñāna is the effect.
Chapter Ten: The Four Conditions. The Treatise says:

In the first dependent origination, where all phenomena and consciousness act as mutual causes and conditions for one another, what kind of condition do they constitute in the second dependent origination?
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, by how many conditions are these six consciousnesses produced?
Namely, the dominant condition, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

These three types of dependent origination—namely, that which exhausts saṃsāra, that which pertains to the agreeable and disagreeable, and that which pertains to the experience of rebirths—each possess four conditions.
The commentary states:

"Regarding these three types of dependent origination that exhaust saṃsāra, pertain to the agreeable and disagreeable, and involve experience, they each possess four conditions," etc.; within the first type of dependent origination, the ālayavijñāna serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for all phenomena that consist of habitual perfumings (*vāsanā*).

In the second type of dependent origination, ignorance and the other factors serve as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*); because of the dominance of ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise, and so forth.
Furthermore, the six types of consciousness are called "dependent origination as experience," for they possess all three types of conditions.

Among these, for visual consciousness, the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) is the eye; the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is visible form; and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the consciousness that has ceased in the immediate past, which gives rise to the subsequent consciousness.
If the preceding consciousness does not relinquish its locus, then the subsequent consciousness cannot arise.
The same applies to the various classes of consciousness, such as those of the ear and so forth.
Chapter Eleven: Defilement by Afflictions. The Treatise states:

Having thus established the specific name and characteristics of the *ālayavijñāna*, how is it known that this specific name and these characteristics refer exclusively to the *ālayavijñāna* and not to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)?

If one were to exclude the *ālayavijñāna* that is to be established, neither the defiled nor the pure would be possible; specifically, the defilement of afflictions (*kleśasaṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karmasaṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*janmasaṃkleśa*) would all fail to be established, as would worldly and supramundane purity.
Why is it that the defilement by afflictions cannot be established?
Because the seeds perfumed by the primary afflictions and secondary afflictions within the six groups of consciousness cannot be established.

For example, when visual consciousness arises and ceases simultaneously with afflictions and secondary afflictions such as desire, it is this very visual consciousness that is perfumed to form the seeds of those [afflictions], and not anything else.
If this very visual consciousness has ceased and other consciousnesses arise in its place, neither the perfuming nor that upon which the perfuming depends can be found, because they do not exist.

When visual consciousness has first ceased and other consciousnesses arise in succession, there is no possibility of their arising simultaneously with desire; because it is past, such a state cannot be established.
It is like a karma that has already perished: the production of its retribution cannot be accomplished.
Furthermore, the perfuming of the visual consciousness that arises simultaneously with desire cannot be established.
This perfuming does not reside within the desire itself, because desire depends upon the consciousness and is not stable.
Nor does it reside within other consciousnesses, because each consciousness has its own distinct basis and because they do not arise and perish simultaneously.
Nor does it reside within its own substance, because within a single substance two consciousnesses cannot arise and perish together.
Therefore, the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as desire cannot perfume the visual consciousness.
Nor can the perfuming of consciousness by consciousness be established, just as it is with the visual consciousness;
it should be understood that the same applies to the remaining evolving consciousnesses.
The commentary states:

Thus, having already explained the various names of the ālayavijñāna and established its characteristics, we now wish to establish that these two [characteristics] reside within the ālayavijñāna alone and not within any other consciousness; therefore, they are demonstrated through reasoning.

Just as visual consciousness arises and ceases simultaneously with afflictions such as desire, it is this very visual consciousness—not any other—that is perfumed by them to form seeds; therein, "this very [consciousness]" refers to visual consciousness.
"That" refers to greed and so forth.
"Forming the seed" means serving as the cause.
"Not others" means not being the auditory consciousness or other such cognitions.
"Perceived by other consciousnesses" refers to the auditory consciousness and so forth being separated [from the object].
"Impregnation" (vāsanā) refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of craving and so forth.
"The basis of impregnation" refers to the visual consciousness.
That which arises simultaneously with greed means that it arises at the same time as greed and so forth; because it is past, it cannot function as a cause.
Just as a result cannot be further produced from a karma that has already ceased, this too cannot be established.
Furthermore, there are Vaibhāṣika masters who hold this view:
they wish to maintain that the past exists as a real entity.
However, that which is past possesses only a name; the referent it signifies cannot be apprehended.
Why is this so? If a phenomenon were existent [in the present], how could it be past?
Therefore, that position regarding the fruit is untenable, because there would be no perfuming.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that the habitual perfuming (vāsanā) of visual consciousness arising simultaneously with desire cannot be established:

this means that even the self-perfuming of this very visual consciousness arising simultaneously with desire cannot be established; how then could it be possible for this visual consciousness to maintain the perfuming so that desire and other states arise?
Furthermore, it does not exist within desire; that is to say, there is no logical basis for the impression (*vāsanā*) of visual consciousness to exist within desire. Why is this?
Because desire depends upon visual consciousness, and furthermore, because it does not abide stably.
"Nor does it exist within other consciousnesses" means that because their bases (*āśraya*) are distinct—namely, the auditory consciousness and so forth—the same arising and ceasing cannot occur.

Precisely because their bases are distinct, the visual consciousness depends on the eye as its own basis, the auditory consciousness depends on the ear as its own basis, and so on, up to the mental consciousness which depends on the mind as its own basis.
Because they occupy distinct locations, it is not possible for one consciousness to perfuse another consciousness.

Furthermore, it does not reside within its own substance; that is to say, a visual consciousness cannot perfume that very same visual consciousness, because two visual consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.
Since two consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, there is no simultaneous arising and simultaneous ceasing.

By this principle, the perfuming of afflictions and secondary afflictions such as desire within visual consciousness is not established; furthermore, even the perfuming of visual consciousness by visual consciousness itself cannot be established.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, when one who has descended from the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) is born in this world, at the moment the first consciousness arises—tainted by the afflictions (kleśa) and secondary afflictions (upakleśa)—this [consciousness] arises without seeds, because both the perfuming (vāsanā) and its support (āśraya) have already passed away and no longer exist.
The commentary states:
"The first" refers to the very first arising consciousness.
"Arising without seeds" means arising without a cause.
Regarding "perfuming and the basis," this refers to the mind and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, when the consciousness that serves as the antidote to the afflictions arises, all mundane consciousnesses are extinguished.

If the ālaya-vijñāna did not exist, the seeds of the afflictions and secondary afflictions would not constitute a self-substance within the counteractive consciousness; consequently, liberation could not arise and cease simultaneously with the afflictions.

If, at a later time, worldly consciousness arises while the mind free from desire no longer exists, its support and its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) would have long since perished; thus, apart from the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it would have to arise without a seed.
Therefore, apart from the ālayavijñāna, neither the afflictions nor the secondary afflictions can be established.
The commentary states:
"When the consciousness that serves as the antidote to the afflictions arises, all worldly consciousnesses cease" means that all six consciousnesses cease.

Regarding the fact that the seeds of the afflictions and secondary afflictions do not exist within the counteractive consciousness (*pratipakṣa-vijñāna*): this means that it is impossible for worldly consciousness to arise with the counteractive consciousness as its cause.
"At a later time" refers to after the supramundane mind.
"The basis and the perfuming" means that the basis is consciousness itself, while the perfuming refers to that which is perfumed by the afflictions and secondary afflictions, and so forth.
"Being without seeds" means arising without a cause, apart from the ālayavijñāna.
Within that state, afflictions would be defilements; for this reason, the defilement by afflictions could not be established.
Chapter Twelve: On the Defilement of Karma. The treatise states:
How is it that the defilement of karma is not established?
Because the condition of *saṃskāra* for *vijñāna* is not established, and because this does not exist, the condition of *upādāna* for *bhava* is likewise not established.
The commentary states:
Now, it is further demonstrated that the defilement of karma cannot be established.
In what way is it not established?

Since it is impossible for formations to have consciousness as their condition, once meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations have arisen and subsequently ceased, where could their perfuming (vāsanā) be deposited apart from the ālayavijñāna?
The six groups of consciousness cannot sustain the perfuming; this point has already been explained in the section on the defilement of afflictions.
Because this [sustaining] does not exist, it follows that consciousness conditioned by formations is not established, and thus existence conditioned by grasping is likewise not established.
Why is this? Because there are causes and conditions.
The various formations (saṃskāra) perfuse consciousness by the power of grasping (upādāna).
Because the perfuming reaches fulfillment and transforms into existence, karma therein is itself defilement; this is called "karmic defilement.
Furthermore, because there is defilement by means of karma, it is called "karmic defilement."
Therefore, the defilement of karma is not established.
Chapter Thirteen: The Defilement of Birth. The Treatise says:
How is it that the defilement of birth is not established?
Because rebirth-linking would otherwise be impossible:

if one falls into or dwells in an unpeaceful realm, there is a defiled mental consciousness that performs the rebirth-linking; this defiled mental consciousness ceases within the intermediate state (antarābhava), and the consciousness then unites with the kalala in the mother’s womb.

If it were only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises through conjunction, and having arisen through conjunction, this consciousness were to serve as the basis for the further arising of the mental consciousness within the mother’s womb, then two instances of mental consciousness would be arising simultaneously in the same location within the womb.
The arising of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) through that conjunction of conditions cannot be established, because mental consciousness is always dependent upon a defiled basis,
and because its objective referent (*ālambana*) is likewise unobtainable.

Suppose this mental consciousness were to combine with the red and white [elements]: would this combined consciousness itself be the "all-seed" (sarvabījaka), or would it be that other consciousnesses arise based upon this consciousness, which then serves as the all-seed?

If that very combination of consciousnesses were the possessor of all seeds, it would be the ālayavijñāna itself; you have merely established a different name for it, calling it "mental consciousness."
If that which serves as the basis for the arising of consciousness is the storehouse of all seeds, while its supporting causal substance is not, this is logically untenable.

For this reason, it is established that this associated consciousness is not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), but rather the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), because it is the possessor of all seeds (*sarvabījaka*).
The commentary states:
The arising of defilement is impossible apart from the *ālayavijñāna*; this point shall now be demonstrated.
"Failure to achieve rebirth-linking" means that one does not attain a new body.
"The non-quiescent realm" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Falling" refers to the end of life.
The "defiled mental consciousness" refers to the mental consciousness being accompanied by afflictions.

Regarding "taking birth," because it appropriates one's own body, that defiled mental consciousness takes the state of existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) as its object, and thus the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) immediately ceases.

Regarding "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*): because they are equally established in both arising and ceasing through a single characteristic, it means that when consciousness conjoins with the red and white [elements], based upon that conjunction, consciousness gives rise to further consciousness.

Regarding the coexistence of two consciousnesses: this refers to the simultaneous presence at one time of both the synthetic mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the distinct mental consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that arises based upon it, because these two consciousnesses exist together at the same moment.
Furthermore, that consciousness which is a composite cannot be established as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Why?
Because it is always defiled and serves as its basis.

That synthetic mental consciousness (manovijñāna), being defiled by afflictions such as desire, takes the afflicted mind (kliṣṭa-manas) as its support and grasps at the arising of existence; because it is defiled, it is said to "have the afflicted as its support" by virtue of depending upon this.
This consciousness abiding in the womb does not take defilement as its support, because its retributive substance is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

As for the claim that "the objects apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot be found here," when the mental consciousness apprehends objects, it can indeed find what are called "all phenomena" (*dharmas*); however, this combined consciousness has no such apprehension. Therefore, it cannot be established that this is the mental consciousness.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, once rebirth has been linked, it is the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) that maintains the sense faculties (*rūpindriya*); otherwise, there would be no possibility for such maintenance, because the other various consciousnesses each rely on distinct bases and do not abide stably.
However, the various material sense-faculties do not exist without consciousness.
The commentary explains:
"Having already undergone rebirth" means that one has already obtained a body.

If they were different, it would mean that once the ālayavijñāna has been relinquished, the other six consciousnesses would each occupy separate locations and be subject to movement; just as visual consciousness invariably relies solely upon the eye, so too would the other consciousnesses each rely individually upon their respective supports, such as the ear and other material sense organs.

If the ālayavijñāna did not exist, and these various consciousnesses each maintained their own supporting sense organs, then because these consciousnesses are subject to fluctuation and may at times be absent, the eyes and other organs would lack maintenance and should consequently decay and rot.
The Treatise says:
"Consciousness and name-and-form depend upon each other, like bundles of reeds leaning against one another; this principle is not established.
The Commentary explains:
Now, I wish to demonstrate this meaning of non-establishment.
As the Blessed One has said:
"Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form; name-and-form is the condition for consciousness."
Regarding "among these, consciousness is the condition for name": "name" refers to the six groups of consciousness;
that is to say, it refers to the four non-material aggregates. "Form," on the other hand, is the *kalala*.
Regarding the consciousness that has name-and-form as its object, if the ālayavijñāna did not exist, what would it be?
It is by depending upon name-and-form that [consciousness] arises in a continuous succession from moment to moment without interruption.
The treatise says:
If one were apart from the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the food of consciousness for all sentient beings would not be established.
Apart from this retributive consciousness, none of the six consciousnesses could accomplish the function of food among all sentient beings within the three realms.
The commentary states:
These words demonstrate that the "consciousness-food" (vijñānāhāra) is untenable.
The Blessed One taught four kinds of nutriment:
First, edible food; second, contact; third, mental volition; fourth, consciousness.
As for "edible," it has the characteristic of transformation; having undergone transformation, it is able to perform the function of sustaining and benefiting the body.
Contact has the characteristic of the objective field; for example, objective fields such as visible forms can benefit the body simply through seeing them and so forth.
Volition has the characteristic of recollection; it benefits the body solely by means of recollection, just as one who is thirsty sees water and thereby avoids death.

Consciousness has the characteristic of sustaining; because of this sustaining, the body remains alive. If this consciousness were absent, the body would be like a corpse, putrid and decaying. Therefore, one should know that consciousness is also called "nutriment," because it is capable of bringing benefit to the body.

Among these, the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*) consists of the six groups of consciousness; the food of mental volition (*manaḥsañcetanā*) is the mind that recollects. Since it has already been stated that there is the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), we know that there must be a distinct consciousness [apart from the six].

Furthermore, in cases such as deep sleep, the absence of mind, fainting, or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the six groups of consciousness have ceased; what else could then maintain the body so that it does not rot and decay?
Because when the ālayavijñāna is abandoned, the body then decays and perishes.
The treatise says:
If one has fallen from this [state] and is born in a higher, tranquil stage, it is by means of the defiled and non-tranquil manovijñāna that one binds oneself to that birth.
In those stages, the non-quiescent and defiled mind cannot have its seeds found if it were apart from the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
The commentary states:
It has already been explained that rebirth-linking is not established in the non-quiescent stages; now, the non-establishment [of rebirth] in the quiescent stages shall be demonstrated.
In this case, that birth is bound by defiled consciousness; even in a tranquil stage (*śānta-bhūmi*), it is likewise bound by defiled non-tranquility.
It is "defiled" because it is defiled by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that stage.

Regarding the afflictions of that stage, these refer to attachment to the flavor of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rasa*) and so forth; such defilements exist precisely within the non-quiescent stages (*aśānta-bhūmi*).
If this person dies in a non-quiescent stage, once they have died, how can the mind of a higher stage manifest?
Since it does not manifest before one's eyes, how could it bring about the linking of that birth?

Therefore, it must certainly exist as the *ālayavijñāna*; because the mind containing the perfumations (*vāsanā*) of those stages exists from beginningless time, through these perfumations, that mind manifests and brings about the linking of that birth.
The treatise states:

Even if one is born in the formless realm, all defiled and wholesome minds would lack seeds and a locus of subsistence if they were separated from the retributive consciousness that contains all seeds. Therefore, these defiled and wholesome minds would be impossible.
The commentary states:
"Those born in the formless realm" refers to those who have attained liberation from the realm of form.
"Defiled and wholesome minds" refers to relishing the flavor of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"Without seeds and without a place of abiding" means without cause and without support.
There is another meaning:
if there are no seeds, by what cause would [phenomena] arise?
If there were no place of abiding, how could it abide by depending upon anything?
Because that mind is sustained by the ālayavijñāna, it arises from its own seeds; it thus depends upon this consciousness, and because there is this dependence, it is able to continue in succession.
The treatise says:
If, within that very realm, supramundane mind manifests and all other mundane minds are extinguished, one should then pass away from that destiny.
The commentary states:

Within that very state, when supramundane consciousness manifests, with the exception of that supramundane consciousness alone, all other minds are mundane. Because those various mundane minds no longer exist, one severs that destiny; this is precisely attaining nirvana without remainder without relying on further effort.
Since this principle does not exist, it is impossible [to account for the process] apart from the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
The treatise states:

"If one is born among the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and the supramundane mind manifests based upon the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), then one should immediately abandon both destinies."

This supramundane consciousness does not rely upon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor does it rely upon the sphere of nothingness; even its reliance upon the sphere of nirvana is not established.
The commentary states:

If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are times when a supramundane mind based on the sphere of nothingness manifests before one; this is because the mind of that [lower] stage is clear and sharp, whereas the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is dull.

When the supramundane mind manifests through the cultivation of a clear and sharp mind, that supramundane mind cannot rely upon either the first or the second destinies, because both of these stages are mundane.
Furthermore, it is also untenable for a mind belonging to one stage to manifest while depending on a body born in another stage, because the body remains as a residual basis.
Nor is it tenable for this mind to take nirvana as its basis.
Since these three kinds of bases are thus untenable, if one were apart from the *ālaya-vijñāna*, in what would this supramundane mind abide?
The treatise says:

When a person performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds, at the time of death, if they were apart from the *ālaya-vijñāna*, the gradual cooling of the body—whether from the top down or from the bottom up—could not occur.
Therefore, if one were separated from the resultant consciousness containing all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vipākavijñāna*), the arising of defilement would also be impossible.
The commentary states:

Within this [system], when one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds, there occurs a difference in the cooling of the body from the top down or from the bottom up; for those who perform wholesome deeds ascend, while those who commit evil fall downward.
Therefore, if the existence of the ālayavijñāna as the sustainer were not admitted, how could this body become cold?

It is because the ālayavijñāna acts as the sustainer that it is gradually relinquished, either from the top down or from the bottom up; at each point where it is relinquished, that part becomes a corpse, and thus the body becomes cold.
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Two;

Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
