The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not saṃsāra, because its perfected aspect (*pariniṣpanna-bhāga*) is precisely nirvāṇa;
nor is it nirvāṇa, because its imagined aspect (*parikalpita-bhāga*) constitutes saṃsāra. Therefore, one must not speak of it as being exclusively one part or the other.

The World-Honored One perceives that within the dependent nature there is no partiality toward a single identity; with this intention, he taught in that sutra that one neither perceives saṃsāra nor perceives nirvāṇa.
The treatise says:
As the Blessed One stated in the Abhidharma-sūtra, there are three categories of phenomena: the defiled portion, the purified portion, and that which belongs to both portions.
On what basis is this stated?

Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) constitutes the defiled portion, while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) constitutes the pure portion; thus, this very dependent nature is those two portions. It is on this basis that such a statement is made.
By what analogy is this meaning illustrated?
It is illustrated by the analogy of a gold-bearing earth deposit.
Just as a gold-bearing earth deposit has three visible aspects—namely, first, the element of earth; second, the soil; and third, the gold.
Within the earth element, soil does not exist yet is visible, whereas gold truly exists yet is not visible.
If one burns it with fire, the soil disappears and the gold becomes manifest.

Furthermore, within the earth element, when the appearance of soil manifests, it is the manifestation of the false; when the appearance of gold manifests, it is the manifestation of the real. Therefore, the earth element has two aspects.

In this way and thus, as long as this nature of consciousness has not been incinerated by the fire of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), the nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) manifests within that consciousness, while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) does not manifest.

If this nature of consciousness is incinerated by the fire of non-conceptual wisdom, the truly existent perfected nature manifests within that consciousness, while the nature of false discrimination does not manifest.
Therefore, this consciousness of false discrimination, whose nature is dependent (*paratantra-svabhāva*), possesses two aspects, just as the earth element exists within gold-bearing soil.
The commentary states:
Thus it is said in the Abhidharma Sūtras:
The imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is the defiled aspect; the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is the pure aspect; and the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is the substance of those two aspects.
For this reason, three kinds of dharmas are taught: namely, the defiled aspect, the pure aspect, and the aspect of both. This is illustrated by the analogy of gold hidden in the earth.

Among these, the "gold-treasure" refers to the seed of gold; the earth element refers to its solid nature; and the soil refers to derived matter. Within the color of the soil, three types may be found.
Within that earth-element, all that exists as gold merely manifests as the appearance of soil; this is known because the substance of that gold can be obtained at a later time. Why is this?
If one burns gold with fire, it becomes manifest; therefore, it is known that gold has existed inherently from the beginning.
The treatise says:
In some places the Blessed One has taught that all phenomena are permanent; in others, he has taught they are impermanent; and in others, he has taught they are neither permanent nor impermanent.
For what purpose did he teach that they are permanent?

Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is said to be permanent with respect to its perfected aspect (*pariniṣpanna-bhāga*); it is said to be impermanent with respect to its imagined aspect (*parikalpita-bhāga*); and it is said to be neither permanent nor impermanent with respect to those two aspects together.

For this reason, it is said that permanence and impermanence are non-dual; suffering and pleasure are also non-dual; the wholesome and the unwholesome are also non-dual; emptiness and non-emptiness are non-dual; self and non-self are non-dual; tranquility and non-tranquility are non-dual; having intrinsic nature and lacking intrinsic nature are non-dual; arising and non-arising are non-dual; cessation and non-cessation are non-dual; primordial stillness and non-primordial stillness are non-dual; natural nirvana and non-natural nirvana are non-dual; and saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are non-dual.
Such distinctions as these—the secret teachings of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—all accord with the three natures, as explained through the gateways of permanence and impermanence.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Just as phenomena have no intrinsic existence, Yet they manifest in infinite varieties."
Neither dharma nor non-dharma, therefore it is said that there is no dual meaning.
Based on one aspect, it is revealed as either existent or non-existent;
based on two aspects, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.
Because they do not exist as they appear, they are said to be non-existent;
because they appear in this way, they are said to be existent.
They are self-manifesting yet devoid of intrinsic being, for their own essence does not abide.
Since grasping does not exist, it is established as being without intrinsic nature.
Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is established that the former serves as the basis for the latter:
non-arising and non-ceasing, quiescence, and primordial nirvāṇa.
The commentary states:
Regarding the fact that phenomena, though non-existent, manifest in infinite varieties—the first half-verse corresponds to this sequence as being neither dharma nor non-dharma.
Why is this? Because it is non-existent, it is called "not dharma" (*adharma*); because it is not the case that the manifesting phenomena are non-existent, it is called "not non-dharma.
Because it is neither dharma nor non-dharma, it is said to have the meaning of non-duality.
"One part" means one side.
"Either existent or non-existent" refers to the teaching that it is demonstrated as either the extreme of existence or the extreme of non-existence.

Regarding the statement "neither existent nor non-existent" based on two parts: because the dependent nature possesses these two aspects, it is described as neither existent nor non-existent by taking this meaning into account.
Regarding "that which appears does not exist": the phenomena as they are perceived do not exist; because they are thus, they are said to be non-existent.
Regarding "therefore it is said to exist": for this very reason, it is said to exist.
Now, the intention behind the teaching of the absence of intrinsic nature shall be revealed.
Regarding "not existing by itself": because no phenomenon exists that can exist independently of causes and conditions, this constitutes one sense of the absence of intrinsic nature.

The statement that "the essence does not exist" is another sense of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*): if a phenomenon has ceased, its essence does not arise again; therefore, it lacks intrinsic nature.

Regarding "because their own essence does not abide": all phenomena lack the power to remain for even a single moment at the very time of their arising; this too is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). These phenomena that lack intrinsic nature are shared with the Śrāvakas.

If such grasping does not exist, this is not shared with the śrāvakas; because the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) as it is grasped by ordinary beings does not exist in that way, this meaning is called the "dharma of lack of intrinsic nature" within the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, precisely because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), all [characteristics] such as non-arising are established. Why is this? Because they lack intrinsic nature, there is no arising;

because there is no arising, there is no cessation; because there is neither arising nor cessation, they are primordially quiescent (*ādi-śānta*); and because they are primordially quiescent, they are by nature in *nirvāṇa*.
That "the former serves as the basis for the latter" means that the former acts as the cause for the latter.
Chapter Four: On the Meaning of the Four Intentions and the Four Unifications. The Treatise states:
Furthermore, there are four kinds of intentions and four kinds of unified meanings, into which all the Buddha’s words should be followed and integrated.
1. The intention of equality (*samatābhiprāya*), as when it is said:
"In a former time, I was named Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One.
2. The intention of a different time (*kālabhedābhiprāya*), as when it is said:
By reciting and upholding the name of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, one will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, as stated in the sutras:
by merely making a vow, one attains birth in the world of Sukhāvatī.
Third, the meaning of distinct purposes, as stated in the sūtra:
by drawing near to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, one attains the understanding of the Mahāyāna dharma-meanings.
Fourth, according to the inclinations of people's minds; that is to say, for example, one may praise generosity to a certain person, yet later disparage generosity to that same person.
As it is with generosity, so it is with ethical discipline and the other practices.
These are called the four kinds of intention.
The commentary states:
Just as when someone takes up a thing that shares the same characteristics, they say, "That is indeed me," so too is it with the Blessed One.

Because his mind dwells in the *dharmakāya* of equality, he says, "At that time, I was named Vipaśyin and so forth. It is not that Vipaśyin is identical to Śākyamuni Buddha; rather, in this context, the intention is that of equality.

Regarding the "intention for another time": this intention does not mean that one will definitely attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* merely by reciting the Buddha’s name. It is like saying, "One obtains a thousand gold coins with a single gold coin"—how could one obtain them in a single day?
This intention is directed toward attainment at another time, because that single coin serves as the cause for obtaining a thousand coins.
In this very way, it should be understood that the intention of merely making a vow to be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss is likewise so.

Regarding the attainment of understanding of the Mahāyāna within the intended meaning of another sense: this refers to personally realizing the characteristics of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) through their underlying principles.

If the Blessed One’s intention were such that the meaning could be understood merely according to the literal words, then even ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) would correctly understand it; however, since the realization of that meaning necessarily comes only through drawing near to immeasurable Buddhas, this is the Buddha’s intended meaning.

Regarding those who follow the inclinations of others' minds: for some person they may praise giving, while for another person they may disparage giving; in such a manner, their intentions are fulfilled according to the needs of those individuals.
If a person is stingy, one may praise giving in their presence;
yet if that person has already attained superior desire for giving, one then disparages giving in their presence.
If such an intention is absent, to either praise or disparage within a single act of giving constitutes a contradiction.
Because of this intention, both praise and blame are entirely appropriate.
One should know that the same applies to ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the other perfections.
"Cultivation by a single portion" refers to mundane cultivation.

Regarding the distinction between *manas* (the mental) and *artha* (the meaning): if the Blessed One speaks with a particular intention in mind, that is called *manas*; whereas that which, by virtue of being definitively expressed, causes one to enter into the Buddha's teaching is called *artha*.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the fourfold meaning of "conjunction": first is the meaning of "causing entry," which refers to how, within the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Mahāyāna, the two natures and their distinctions of person and phenomena are explained according to the principles of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Second is the meaning of the two characteristics, which means that within the characteristics of all dharmas as they are taught, they are all revealed by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Third is the meaning of the remedies, which refers to the teaching of the eighty-four thousand gates of remedial practices (*pratipakṣa-caryā*).
The commentary states:

Regarding the meaning of "causing entry," with respect to both persons and phenomena, one speaks either of their intrinsic nature or of their specific distinctions according to the principles of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), in order to cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha-dharma; this is called the meaning of causing entry.

Regarding the meaning of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): herein, one should explain its characteristics by means of the meaning of characteristics, because of the explanation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Regarding the meaning of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*): this refers to explaining the antidotes to the conduct of sentient beings; that is, explaining the antidotes to the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings, for the purpose of establishing a basis for sentient beings to counteract their afflictions.
The treatise says:
There are four ways of reversing meaning, just as words and syllables with distinct meanings reveal distinct meanings.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
*Asaliśa ramata ye vibhriye sija susiddhi ta jitagra kiliśīnaja susamgita riṣṭha ravaṇḍi bodhimutthama.* Commentary:

Regarding these terms, *asali*—in its manifest meaning—is called "unreal," while in its hidden meaning it is called "immovable. Thus, because it is immovable through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is named *asali*.
*Śramatha* is translated as "generating a sense of respect for meditative concentration.
*Viparyāsa* refers to "inversion" in its explicit meaning, and "reversal" in its implicit meaning.
*Su-siddha* means being well-established within the inverted; because one is well-established therein, one takes what is impermanent to be permanent.
This constitutes an inversion, for it is by being well-established within that inversion of taking the impermanent to be permanent that one so abides.
*Kilikisnāta* means, in its explicit sense, "affliction" (*kleśa*), and in its implicit sense, "arduous toil.
*Su-saṃkliṣṭa* refers to being thoroughly defiled; therefore, the Sūtra says:
"For a long time within saṃsāra, one has been thoroughly defiled by arduous toil."
*Labhadhi bodhim uttamām* means "one shall attain supreme enlightenment," which is easily understood.
The treatise states:
If one wishes to explain the Mahāyāna Dharma, it should briefly be explained by means of three characteristics.
First, the explanation of dependent origination; second, the explanation of phenomena produced by causes and conditions; third, the explanation of the meaning within the teachings.
Regarding the explanation of dependent origination therein, as stated in the verse:
"Phenomena produced by the perfuming of speech, these [in turn] act likewise upon that."
This demonstrates that the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise by serving as mutual conditions for one another.

Regarding those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, the evolving consciousness constitutes their characteristic; it possesses the nature of both the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*).
Through the characteristic of abiding, the characteristic of differentiation, and the characteristic of natural law, these three natures are thereby manifested.
As the verse says:
"The characteristic of the object and the characteristic of the vision— these should be known as the three characteristics."
Furthermore, how is that characteristic explained?

It means that the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) has no essence within the dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), whereas the perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) exists within the dependent. Because of these two, non-existence and existence, the unobtainable and the obtainable, not seeing reality and seeing reality—these two occur simultaneously.

Furthermore, within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is non-existent, while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) exists; thus, one attains that [perfected nature] but not this [imagined nature], and does not attain this [imagined nature] but attains that [perfected nature].
As the verse says:
The dependent nature is without conceptual differentiation; Only the perfected nature exists.
Neither the unattainable nor the attainable— Within it, these two are equal.
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "dharmas produced by perfuming," this refers to external conceptualizations that perfume the ālayavijñāna; these reside within consciousness itself. Taking this perfuming as their cause, all dharmas are produced, which constitutes the very nature of the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna).

"The same applies to this with respect to that" means that this perfuming by discrimination takes those various dharmas as its cause; this demonstrates that the *ālayavijñāna* and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) serve as mutual causes for one another.

Furthermore, regarding all phenomena that constitute the nature of the arising consciousness, which have the essence of consciousness characterized by both aspect (nimitta) and vision (darśana): this means that if the essence of consciousness possesses both aspect and vision, it is precisely that [consciousness] itself.
These phenomena possess three characteristics; that which is called the characteristic of abiding and maintaining is precisely the dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).
Through these explanations, the characteristics inherent in the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are thereby made manifest.
These and other such meanings are manifested through the meaning of the verses as having both aspect (*nimitta*) and vision (*darśana*).

One should know that these three characteristics are as revealed in the commentary on the root treatise: namely, non-existence and existence; the unobtainable and the obtainable; and the simultaneous occurrence of not seeing reality and seeing reality—these two being concurrent. These are what is manifested therein.

Regarding these two, namely the conceptualized (parikalpita) and the perfected (pariniṣpanna), because one of these two parts does not exist while the other does exist, they are said to be "existent and non-existent."

If one engages in conceptual discrimination, one will not achieve accomplishment because of failing to see reality; however, at that very time, if one does not engage in conceptual discrimination, one will achieve accomplishment because of seeing reality.
These meanings are further illustrated by verses.
In the verses, the term "equality" refers to [the fact that all things] exist in a single moment.
The phrase "within it" refers to being within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
The second refers to seeing reality and not seeing reality.
"Hence" means because there are causes and conditions.

This is because within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) is non-existent while perfected existence (*pariniṣpanna*) is existent; thus, ordinary worldlings see it through inverted grasping, whereas the noble ones (*ārya*) see it through correct vision (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
The Commentary states:

Regarding the explanation of the meaning within the verbal teachings, it is as when the first phrase is taken as the basis and the remaining phrases are used to reveal its aspects—whether these be the basis for qualities (*guṇa*) or the basis for meaning (*artha*).
Regarding the basis of merit: as it is said, the Buddha’s qualities consist of the most pure awakening,
the non-dual dharma, practicing the signless dharma as the supreme path, abiding in the Buddha-abode, attaining equality with all Buddhas,
reaching the state of non-obstruction, the non-retrogressive dharma, the unimpeded realm, and the inconceivable.
Having established this deliberation, they enter into the equality of the three periods of time;
they possess bodies that pervade all worlds, unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena, complete knowledge of all practices, and are free from doubt regarding the wisdom of the Dharma.
They possess non-conceptual bodies, the wisdom received by all bodhisattvas, and have reached the supreme perfection of the non-dual dwelling of the Buddhas.
Honey, the ultimate non-differentiated liberation-wisdom of the Tathāgata, entry into the boundless and centerless Buddha-ground of the equal Dharma-realm,
the foremost [state] that extends throughout the limits of space, and so forth.

The most pure awakening (*suviśuddhabodhi*) is the foundation; it should be understood that all other phrases are differentiations of this very phrase. Such an exposition is called a "skillful explanation.

Regarding the statement that the essence of all phenomena is the most pure awakening: this refers to the most pure awakening of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and it should be understood as encompassing the remaining twenty-one qualities of a Buddha.

That is to say: the merit of proceeding without any obstruction whatsoever regarding that which is to be known; the merit of the most pure *tathatā* which causes entry into the non-dual characteristic of existence and non-existence;
the merit of the Buddha’s abiding in effortless buddha-activities without cessation;
and the merit of the mental activity being undifferentiated by virtue of taking the *dharmakāya* as its support.
The merit of cultivating the remedies for all obstacles;
the merit of subduing all non-Buddhists;
and the merit of being born in the world without being hindered by worldly dharmas.
The merit of establishing the Dharma;
the merit of bestowing predictions of enlightenment;
and the merit of manifesting the enjoyment body and transformation bodies throughout all worlds.
The merit of severing doubt;
the merit of causing entry into various practices;
and the merit of generating knowledge regarding future phenomena.
The merit of manifesting according to what is desired;
the merit of immeasurable bodies for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
and the merit of accomplishing the *pāramitās* of the equal Dharma-body.
The merit of manifesting the non-differentiation of Buddha-fields according to what one believes and delights in;
the merit of the three bodies of the Buddha being unrestricted by spatial location;
and the merit of constantly acting for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings until the very end of saṃsāra.
"Inexhaustible merit.
The commentary states:
Regarding the "manifestation of its aspects," as should be explained according to the context, this meaning is now being manifested.

It is either subsumed under qualities (*guṇa*) or subsumed under meaning (*artha*). Within that which is subsumed under qualities, "the most pure awakening" is the first phrase, while the remaining phrases reveal its meaning.
Regarding the absence of dualistic practice therein: since dualistic practice cannot be found, it is called non-dual practice.
It is not like the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, which possesses both obstruction and non-obstruction.
That which is the supreme purity of the non-dual nature of existence and non-existence refers to the purified *tathatā* (suchness), which is the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).
This *tathatā* is not characterized by existence, because all phenomena are non-existent;
nor is it characterized by non-existence, because it possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
This *tathatā* (suchness) is the foremost purity within the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).
Because it is the locus of entry, it is said to possess the quality of "causing entry.
Because it is most excellent, it is called the "path" (*mārga*); since "path" carries the meaning of a locus of entry, it is termed the path.
Regarding the merit of the Buddha’s effortless activity and his unceasing abiding: this refers to the fact that he constantly performs all buddha-activities without ever ceasing.
Regarding the merit of cultivating the remedies for all obstacles: because he constantly cultivates awakening at all times, he is able to remedy all hindrances.

Regarding the merit of being born in the world without being obstructed by worldly dharmas: although one who is born in the world must necessarily engage within the sphere of worldly experience, even while living in the world, they are not defiled by the eight worldly concerns, such as gain and so forth.

Regarding the establishment of the merit of the Dharma: the various dharmas such as the sūtras are immeasurable and inconceivable; because ordinary beings cannot enter them, it is called the "most pure awakening."
This very phrase of the most pure awakening is associated with each and every individual phrase.
Regarding the "merit of the wisdom that knows the arising of future phenomena," it means that one is able to know that all phenomena in the future world will arise in such a manner.

Regarding "the merit corresponding to the immeasurable bodies for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings": this refers to the immeasurable bodies of various bodhisattvas when they perform the work of teaching and transforming sentient beings. Because all Buddhas have attained the wisdom of the equality of self and others, and because that wisdom is subsumed within the Buddha-wisdom, it is itself the work of the Buddha’s teaching and transformation.

Regarding the merit of accomplishing the perfection of the equal dharmakāya: it is called "equal" because the dharmakāya is non-dual; by virtue of this non-dual dharmakāya, one attains the most pure perfection.

Regarding "the knowledge of liberation that is ultimately without distinction": this refers to the fact that within the non-discriminative wisdom of the Tathāgata, liberation is ultimate; herein, "liberation" is precisely the supreme liberation (*adhiprajñā*).

Regarding the merit of the three bodies of the Buddha being without spatial limitation or division: this means that the Dharma-body cannot be delimited by various locations; likewise, the Enjoyment-body and the Transformation-body are also thus with respect to all worlds.
Regarding "the foremost of the dharma-realm": because it is the most pure dharma-realm, it is called the foremost of the dharma-realm.
Regarding "exhausting the realm of empty space": because the Buddha’s wisdom is inexhaustible like empty space, it is therefore called the most pure awakening.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, regarding the basis of meaning, as the Sūtra states:
"A Bodhisattva who is endowed with thirty-two qualities is called a Bodhisattva; he gives rise [to these] toward all sentient beings."
Because of the intention to bring benefit and happiness; because of causing [others] to enter the wisdom of all-knowledge;
because of knowing my own worth; because of abandoning pride; because of having a firm resolve; because of showing compassion without any ulterior motive;
because of maintaining an impartial mind toward both friends and enemies; because of being a true friend until the very limit of nirvāṇa; and because it is appropriate in measure.
Because he speaks with purpose; because he smiles before speaking; because his great compassion is boundless; because he bears the heavy burden without retreat or discouragement;
because his mind is free from weariness; because he never tires of hearing the meaning of the Dharma;

because he is able to see the faults of the transgressions he himself has committed; because he instructs others regarding their faults and failings without resentment; and because of all his majestic...
Because one cultivates the bodhicitta within the ritual; because one practices giving without seeking karmic retribution;
because one maintains ethical discipline without relying on rebirth in any realm of existence; because one practices patience toward all sentient beings without obstruction;
because one practices diligence in gathering all wholesome dharmas; and because one cultivates [meditative concentration] while relinquishing the formless realm.
Because of meditative concentration; because of wisdom conjoined with skillful means; because of employing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as the method of gathering [beings];

because of maintaining a state of loving-kindness and compassion toward those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them without distinction; because of reverently listening to the true Dharma; because of reverently dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*);
because of not delighting in or being attached to worldly distractions; and because of [the state of] inferiority...
Because they have no longing for other vehicles, because they perceive the merits within the Mahāyāna, because they distance themselves from evil friends, because they draw near to virtuous friends,
because they purely cultivate the four brahma-vihāras, because they sport in the five supernormal powers,
because they act in accordance with wisdom, and because they do not abandon sentient beings— whether they abide in right conduct or do not abide in right conduct.
Therefore, because it is spoken with single-mindedness, because it emphasizes ultimate reality, and because it takes the bodhicitta as its foremost principle—
these various phrases should be understood as being differentiated from the first phrase.

Regarding the intention to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, it should be understood that this phrase "intention to bring benefit and happiness" comprises sixteen distinct types of activity.
Among these, the sixteen activities are: the activity of successive arising;
non-perverted activity; and so forth.
He performs his activities even without being requested; he performs his activities without wavering or faltering;

and he performs his activities without seeking anything for himself—these are the three phrases. [The latter] is because he does not seek recompense, because he feels neither hatred nor affection toward sentient beings who act contrary to or in accordance with him, and because he follows them through birth after birth.
Within this category, bodily and vocal actions comprise two phrases: actions that are equanimous toward suffering, pleasure, and that which is neither;
non-depreciated actions;
and non-regressive actions.
The activity of grasping skillful means;

the activity of aversion toward obstacles—these consist of two phrases; the activity of uninterrupted reflection and the activity of progressing toward excellence—these consist of seven phrases, comprising the correct practice of the six *pāramitās* and the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);

the activity of accomplishing the cultivation of skillful means—this consists of six phrases: because of associating with virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*), because of hearing the true Dharma, because of dwelling in forest hermitages (*araṇya*), because of distancing oneself from unwholesome thoughts, and because of the two kinds of merit in correct reflection, the two kinds of merit in shared activities, and the three kinds of accomplishment in activity: through immeasurable purity, through attaining great majestic power, and through attaining supreme merit.

The establishment of those karmas consists of four points: because they encompass all meritorious qualities; because they provide definitive instruction; because the two forms of gathering—through Dharma and through material wealth—are treated as one; and because they are free from a defiled mind.
One should understand that all such phrases are distinctions of phrases.
As stated in a verse of the Sūtra:
"Because they are subsumed under the first phrase, they are distinguished by their qualities."
"Because it is subsumed under the first phrase, there is a distinction of meaning and a distinction of phrases.
The commentary states:
"The basis of the meaning refers to the intention for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings."
This phrase has sixteen functions, and other phrases further reveal the intention for benefit and happiness therein.

As for what kind of function causes one to enter the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*): if one causes all sentient beings to enter the knowledge of all-knowledge, this is the successive practice.
For example, just as a single lamp transmits its light to a thousand lamps, this demonstrates the intention for benefit and happiness.
All such phrases are associated with this intention for benefit and happiness.
To think that one knows one's own worth while harboring a desire for personal benefit and happiness is still a form of delusion.

It is like someone who intends to bring benefit and happiness but gives another alcohol to drink; if one teaches sentient beings according to reality and in accordance with their own capacity, rather than out of pride, then even if one has no knowledge oneself, the intention to benefit will not result in harm. However, if one acts otherwise, it conversely becomes a source of no benefit.
One who has abandoned arrogance does so because, having abandoned the mind of arrogance, they preach the Dharma spontaneously without waiting for an exhortation.
One whose will is firm does not allow the resolve for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings to be shaken or destroyed by their deluded conduct.
It is not that he forms an intention of compassion for some specific purpose, because he does not act for the sake of gain and honor when benefiting sentient beings.
How can this intention of benefit and happiness be known?

Because they consist of bodily and vocal actions performed in accordance with [the Dharma], therein, speaking in moderation and being the first to speak are vocal actions; smiling and possessing boundless great compassion are bodily actions.
In this context, "measured speech" refers to speaking only that which is appropriate for the task.
"Unlimited compassion" refers to pitying [beings] because of the three types of suffering.
"Suffering" refers to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Pleasure is so called because it is subject to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Neither-pain-nor-pleasure is so called because it is subject to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
That which is neither of the two is so called because it is neither painful nor pleasant.
Regarding "not engaging in base actions," this means not disparaging oneself by thinking, "I cannot become a Buddha," and so forth.
Regarding "having no sense of weariness," if one is free from fatigue, one is able to cultivate the path to Buddhahood.
"One who never tires of hearing the Dharma": if one does not hear much, one will lack the skillful wisdom for teaching and transforming sentient beings.
"In all modes of deportment": the meaning of this phrase is as explained in the *Śuddhacaryā-sūtra*.
Advancing in superior activity is the intention for benefit and happiness, because it tends toward the essence of the cause for growth.
Regarding the six phrases concerning the accomplishment of the skillful means of cultivation: if a person draws near to this practice, they will attain accomplishment.
"Respectfully dwelling in an araṇya" means that by residing in such a place, one is able to remain free from evil.
"Perceiving worldly diversions" refers to things such as singing, dancing, and various forms of entertainment.
"One who has accomplished the task" refers to manifesting the signs of such accomplishment.
"Majestic power" refers to the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

"Acting in accordance with wisdom" means acting according to wisdom rather than consciousness, because it arises from one's own wisdom; through this wisdom, there is correct realization and correspondence.
Regarding "establishing those activities within all phenomena": because of the intention for benefit and happiness, one is able to establish sentient beings in benefit and happiness.

Within this, "gathering the assembly" means not abandoning or expelling those who have broken their precepts, but rather establishing them [in virtue], causing them to leave unwholesome states and join with what is wholesome.

Regarding the definitive instruction: because one consistently provides established admonitions and does not, after having spoken oneself, later say "what I previously said was incorrect," the listener receives the teaching.

Regarding "gathering through material things and the Dharma": it means gathering them by speaking to them with sincerity and providing material benefits such as the Dharma, robes, and other necessities; thus, one is "fully endowed with gathering. Regarding "an undefiled mind":

it means that while practicing the gathering of the bodhicitta to perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, one does not seek offerings for oneself, but rather thinks, "How can I cause these sentient beings to attain perfect, unsurpassed enlightenment through this merit? It is because one gathers [others] in this manner.
The meaning within the verse is likewise so.
This concludes the explanation of the characteristics of what is to be known (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*). *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Five.
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Six.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guptadatta of India together with Xingjue and others during the Sui Dynasty.
3. Entry into the Superior Characteristics and Superior Discourse on What is to be Known. Third Treatise. It is said:
Thus far, the characteristics of what is to be known have been explained. How is the entry into these characteristics of what is to be known to be perceived?
It is the basis perfumed by extensive learning, not comprised within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, yet functions as a seed like the *ālaya*.

It is comprised within correct reflection (*samyak-manasikāra*), and is a mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that appears as an object of apprehension, arising from what resembles the dharma and what resembles its meaning, and which possesses an aspect (*sākāra*).
The commentary states:

One should understand that such characteristics as these are to be entered into accordingly; it is for the purpose of revealing this that one enters into the characteristics of the knowable (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*).
"Taking the cultivation of hearing as a support" means taking the body perfumed by the Mahāyāna Dharma as the basis.
That which is not subsumed under the *ālaya* refers to its being the antidote to the *ālayavijñāna*.

Just as the *ālayavijñāna* functions as a seed, so too does this [consciousness] function as the cause of pure phenomena (*śukladharma*), just as the *ālayavijñāna* is the cause of defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*).
That which is subsumed by right reflection refers to its intrinsic nature as right reflection.
That which arises from what resembles the dharma and what resembles the meaning refers to its arising from the signs (*nimitta*) of the dharma and the meaning.

That which resembles the apprehended object refers to its having the same substance as form and so forth; that which possesses vision likewise resembles the substance of vision. This constitutes the establishment of the two consciousnesses: the aspect (nimitta) and the vision (darśana).
The Commentary says:
Among these, which persons are able to enter the characteristics of what is to be known?

They are the bodhisattvas whose mental continuums have been thoroughly perfumed by extensive hearing of the Mahāyāna; who have attained proximity to immeasurable supramundane Buddhas; who possess exclusive faith and understanding and have well accumulated roots of virtue; and who have fully perfected the provisions of merit and wisdom.
The commentary states:

As for the question of who can enter the characteristics of what is to be known (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*), the various skillful means for entering within such categories of characteristics shall now be demonstrated.
"One who has been permeated by extensive learning in the Mahāyāna" is mentioned in order to distinguish them from those who have extensively studied the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.
"Attaining the opportunity to draw near to immeasurable supramundane Buddhas" means that one is able to personally attend and serve all the Buddhas who appear in the world beyond measure.
"Resolutely believing and understanding" means having definitive faith and comprehension within the Mahāyāna, such that one cannot be shaken or corrupted by evil associates.

Thus, because they have well accumulated roots of goodness within the three causal conditions previously described, they are called bodhisattvas who have well accumulated the provisions of merit and wisdom.
Furthermore, how are these provisions of merit and wisdom to be fulfilled in successive order?
This is due to the power of causes, the power of virtuous friends, the power of reflection, and the power of support.
Among these, the first two phrases constitute two powers, which should be understood according to their respective numbers.

The power of that right reflection is precisely single-minded faith and understanding; this takes the cultivation of the Mahāyāna as its cause. This single-minded faith and understanding is itself the practice of correct conduct. Because one practices correct conduct, one gathers roots of goodness; and by the power of this right reflection, one attains the full perfection of the provisions of merit and wisdom.
There is this sequence: because one has thus fully perfected the accumulations of merit and wisdom, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva; this is the power of the support.
The treatise asks:
Into what does one enter?

This is because, within that very state, there is the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that appears as phenomena (*dharma*) and objects (*artha*), which arises from the characteristics of the Mahāyāna teachings.
The commentary states:
Having entered into such characteristics, the mode of entry into this practice shall now be demonstrated.
Mental discrimination on the level of the mind is called "mental discourse" (*manojalpa*); this type of mental discourse arises with the Mahāyāna Dharma as its cause.
That which is produced by the characteristics of the Mahāyāna Dharma takes the taught Dharma as its object of perception.
The treatise says:

Within the stage of practice through resolute belief, within the path of seeing, within the path of cultivation, and within the ultimate path, all phenomena are consciousness-only—because one believes and understands according to what has been heard, because one penetrates reality as it is, because one counteracts all obstacles, and because there is no longer any obstruction.
The commentary states:
Where does one enter?

One enters within the stage of resolute belief (*adhimukti-bhūmi*), because by merely hearing that all phenomena are nothing but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), one gives rise to superior resolute belief; this is called "entering."
The entry into the path of seeing shall now be demonstrated.
"Thoroughly penetrating according to reality" means thoroughly penetrating within the conceptualization of mental discourse according to reality.
What is thorough penetration according to reality?
It is that which is neither dharma nor meaning, being without a grasper and nothing grasped; it is so called because it is the thorough penetration of the conceptualization of mental verbalization.
The entry attained within the path of cultivation shall now be demonstrated.

Regarding the phrase "because it serves as the antidote to all obstacles": when one contemplates these mental expressions (*manojalpa*) as being neither phenomena (*dharma*) nor objects (*artha*), and realizes there is no grasper (*grāhaka*) and nothing grasped (*grāhya*), one is able to counteract all obstacles; this is called the entry attained within the path of cultivation.
The entry into the ultimate path shall now be demonstrated. Regarding the phrase "because of being unobstructed":
it is because one abides in the state of most pure wisdom, and because even the most subtle obscurations have been extinguished; thus, it is called "entry into the ultimate path."
The treatise says: By what causes and conditions does one attain entry?

It is because of being sustained by the power of the roots of goodness; because of the threefold refinement of the mind; because of the elimination of the four bases; because of taking the meaning of the Dharma as the object of focus; and because of the constant and thorough cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, free from negligence, and so forth.
In immeasurable worlds, immeasurable beings among the human realm attain perfect awakening to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* moment by moment; this is the first refinement of the mind.
The commentary states:
By what means does one attain entry?
It is through the eight points of correspondence, such as being sustained by the power of the roots of goodness as previously described.
In this regard, "constant cultivation" means practicing at all times;
"thorough cultivation" means practicing with reverence.
To act in such a manner is itself non-negligence, as it serves to counteract the three types of despondency within that context.
There are three kinds of mental training: when a bodhisattva hears that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is supremely profound, vast, and difficult to realize, his mind may become discouraged and retreat.
To counteract this, there is the first refinement of the mind, and so forth.
Furthermore, because of [the aforementioned] reasons, there is the second refinement of the mind.
The treatise says:
"By means of single-minded concentration, one is able to practice the various pāramitās such as generosity.
I have already attained this single-minded concentration; therefore, it will not be difficult for me to cultivate the pāramitās until they reach full perfection."
This is the second training of the mind.
The commentary states:
It is by means of this mental factor that the perfections such as generosity become manifest; herein, "mental factor" refers to faith (*śraddhā*) and aspiration (*chanda*).
Because the bodhisattva truly knows that the perfections exist, possess merit, and are attainable, this constitutes the bodhisattva’s faith.

Through this faith, the joy and delight in practice is called aspiration (*chanda*). Because the bodhisattva attains this faith and aspiration, they practice the six perfections; they advance toward their fulfillment without regarding it as difficult.
The Treatise says:
Although those who possess obstructed goodness, once their wholesome qualities are complete, obtain at the time of death a body endowed with all things according to whatever they desire;
how much more so for me, who possess this most supreme and unobstructed goodness—why should I not obtain everything complete at that time!
This is called the third refinement of the mind.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Among those in the human realm, there are immeasurable sentient beings."
Attaining enlightenment in every thought-moment, one thus eliminates the mind of despondency.
A person of virtuous mind who focuses their intent can practice giving and the like;
a superior person who attains this intent is likewise able to practice giving and the like.
When a virtuous person dies, they receive the fruit of their actions according to their mind;
since there is already goodness at the moment of cessation, how could there be no fruit?
The commentary explains:
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva investigates the profound and vast teachings of the Buddhas, they reflect:
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to realize; it is attained only after the mind has been severed for even a single kṣaṇa."
One immediately gives rise to despondency.
To counteract this, one cultivates the third refinement of the mind:
"How much more so for me, who am most excellent and virtuous; how much more so for me, who am fully endowed with the provisions of merit and wisdom throughout all ten stages."

Regarding "wholesome without obstruction": this refers to the mind’s afflictions being so subtle and difficult to shatter that they are like a diamond; yet samādhi can shatter these obstructions. Once this samādhi has emerged from all obstructions and the basis [of existence] has been transformed, how could one not attain it?
This reveals that the obstacles to renunciation are no different from death itself.
"Possessing everything" means having attained all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) and being sustained by the power of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).

Regarding the three ways of refining the mind: because their roots of goodness are not meager, Bodhisattvas possess this power by which they can refine their minds in these three ways so that they do not become discouraged or retreat.
Among these, the second is the training of the mind; this training shall now be explained.

By means of this mindfulness, one becomes free from all obstacles; since there are no longer obstructions to the perfections such as stinginess, the fulfillment of the perfections is not difficult, and through this fulfillment, one attains enlightenment.
The third stage, the refinement of the mind, shall now be elucidated.
Among these, that which is "obstructed virtue" refers to mundane virtue; therefore, it is called obstructed virtue.
This virtue of mine is unobstructed; it is impossible that this virtue would fail to bring about Buddhahood—this meaning is demonstrated by verse.
The verse says, "Therefore, one eliminates the mind of despondency," which means not allowing an inferior mind to abide in the thought, "I am unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
A "wholesome mind" refers to that which is neither unwholesome nor neutral.
Because there exists giving with a neutral mind—for instance, when someone gives with a distracted mind—or when non-Buddhists give with an unwholesome mind.
Furthermore, for one who seeks *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this goodness is most supreme; such a person attains this intention.

Moreover, regarding those who are able to practice giving and so forth, when they attain single-minded concentration therein, there are signs such as these: they are able to cultivate the six *pāramitās* of giving and so on, which means they attain the cessation of obstructive states of mind such as stinginess.
"Those who surpass others" refers to the bodhisattvas because they are supreme.
"Generosity and so forth" refers to the inclusion of the perfections of ethical discipline, wisdom, and the rest.
"Obtaining the fruit of maturation according to one's mind" means obtaining the fruit of maturation up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"Destroying the wholesome" means destroying obstacles.
As for "how could there be no karmic retribution," it refers to the attainment of the Buddha-body.
The treatise says:
Because one remains far removed from the contemplations of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, such contemplation is extinguished;
because one is free from all doubt regarding the Mahāyāna, perverse intent and doubt are extinguished;
and because one is free from the grasping at "self" and "mine" within the teachings heard and contemplated, attachment to phenomena is extinguished.
Because one contemplates without conceptualizing all manifest and established signs that abide before one, conceptualization is extinguished.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Established and self-abiding, All manifest signs—"
Without making any conceptual distinctions whatsoever, the wise person attains supreme awakening.
Commentary:
Herein, the root text of the treatise is intended to reveal the cessation of the four bases.
Regarding the cessation of conceptualization therein: this refers to the cessation of the conceptualizations of the śrāvakas and others.
Regarding the cessation of wrong views and doubt: this refers to the fact that within the profound and vast Dharma of the Mahāyāna, wrong views and doubt must be eliminated.
"Wrong intention" refers to a mind of disparagement and mental instability. "Delusion" refers to a doubting mind.
Regarding the phrase "because all doubt is non-doubt":

within this Mahāyāna, in order to establish the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is taught that there are three natures (*trisvabhāva*). These are: that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), neither arising nor ceasing, originally quiescent, and by nature in *nirvāṇa*.
All such dharmas as these are gates of non-existence from the perspective of the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
If one speaks of illusions, mirages, dreams, light, shadows, images, echoes, the moon in water, and transformations, this is from the perspective of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

If one speaks of such gateways as *tathatā* (suchness), *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), *animitta* (signlessness), *paramārtha* (the ultimate truth), *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena), and *śūnyatā* (emptiness), this is because they depend upon the nature of fulfillment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Within these phenomena, all perverse intentions and afflictions do not arise.

Regarding the phrase "because one is free from the grasping at 'I' and 'mine' with respect to the teachings heard and contemplated," this is intended here to demonstrate the elimination of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
To eliminate attachment to phenomena means that, through hearing or contemplating the teachings, one ensures that even the notion of "I" and "mine" does not find entry therein.

Regarding "because one does not conceptually differentiate all mental images that are present, abiding, and established": this means that when a practitioner cultivates non-conceptual wisdom, while in the stage of correct mental attention (*samyak-manasikāra*), they extinguish all such conceptualizations of the tranquil mind.

When one does not attend to or conceptualize any of the signs of the objects—such as the skeletal chains and so forth that are established within the colors and other forms present before one, or within the tranquil mind—at that time, it is called entering the skillful means of non-conceptualization; if one were to conceptualize, one would not enter it.
These verses on the "present establishment" are for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of final cessation.
The treatise asks:
By what cause does one enter?
How does one enter?
Because it is produced by the perfuming of hearing and is subsumed under correct reflection, there arises a mental verbalization that possesses an appearance resembling the dharma and its meaning.
The commentary states:
This demonstrates that one enters by means of this [method] and in this manner.
Among these, that which is produced from the perfuming of hearing arises because the perfuming of hearing serves as its cause; this is precisely the principle of entry.
As previously stated, this arises from the perfuming of hearing the Mahāyāna; it should be understood that it is subsumed within the nature of perfection (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The treatise says:
There are four kinds of seeking, namely: seeking the sign of conventional designation regarding names, meanings, intrinsic natures, and distinctions.
The commentary states:
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the manner of entry herein.
The four kinds of investigation are as stated in the root treatise, namely those concerning name, object, intrinsic nature, and distinction.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, there are four kinds of knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-parijñā*), namely: knowledge as it truly is regarding the conventional designations of names, things, intrinsic natures, and distinctions; for those intrinsic natures and distinctions cannot be apprehended.
In this way, the bodhisattva practices for the sake of entering into the fact that mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Within that mental verbalization which appears as words and meanings, he knows that those names are merely mental verbalization; he knows that the meanings upon which those names depend are also merely mental verbalization. He then realizes that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the distinctions (*viśeṣa*) of those names are merely conventional designations of false appearances (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*). At that time, having realized that there is only mental verbalization, he no longer perceives any substantial nature, distinction, meaning, or characteristic within the conventional designations of names, meanings, intrinsic natures, and distinctions.

Therefore, by means of the fourfold seeking and the fourfold thorough knowledge as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*), one enters into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) within that mental verbalization which appears as names and objects.
The commentary states:

regarding the four thorough knowledges as they truly are, as explained in the treatise, they consist of the thorough knowledge as it truly is of names, things, intrinsic nature, and distinctions within conventional designations.

Regarding "by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and distinctions (*viśeṣa*)," this means that each possesses its own intrinsic nature and distinctions; because they are thus designated by conventional designation, they are called "conventional designations of intrinsic nature and distinctions. Since no objective referent (*artha*) can be found therein, this is precisely knowing that those names, intrinsic natures, and distinctions are merely conventional designations.
Because those names lack intrinsic nature and differentiation, one is able to accept and tolerate that those names, intrinsic natures, and differentiations are merely conventional designations.
If one knows in this way, it is called "seeking"; if one knows that [the object] cannot be attained, it is called "knowing according to reality.
The treatise says:
Into what dharma does this contemplation of consciousness-only enter?
To what kind of phenomena does it correspond?

It corresponds to the entry into "mere-cognition" (vijñapti-mātra), because it consists of the two aspects of the image (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*), and because it possesses various images.

Name, object, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and distinction are merely conventionally established, because the six kinds of entities—namely, intrinsic nature and distinction—are without substantial reality.
Because it exists as the essence of both the grasper and the grasped, and because various phenomena appear simultaneously as if they were manifold characteristics;
just as a rope in the dark appears to be a snake, for example, the snake within the rope is false because it does not exist.
If one perceives the true reality, there is no delusion; the cognition of the snake ceases and only the cognition of the rope remains.

If one analyzes the rope minutely, it too is not real, because it consists of the characteristics of color, odor, taste, and tangibility. Since the cognition of the rope depends upon the cognitions of color and so forth within it, the cognition of the rope can also be eliminated.

In this way, just as the cognition of a snake regarding the sixfold mental verbalization of the semblance of letters and their meanings must be eliminated by knowing that those sixfold aspects lack real meaning, so too must this cognition of consciousness-only be eliminated by means of the cognition of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The commentary states:
Herein, the question concerns the phenomena to be entered and the analogy for entering them.
"Mere-cognition" (vijñaptimātra) refers to the fact that it is merely the cognition of consciousness.

Regarding "the appearance and the seeing constitute the two": this reveals that there are two aspects of consciousness, namely the appearance (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*). Because these appear as if they were appearances, serving as the cause, the locus, the characteristic, and the reflected image, it is simply a single consciousness arising in various forms. It is not that they arise sequentially because of their rapid succession; rather, by means of these three types [of analysis], one enters into *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only).

Regarding the phrase "because at one time there arises an appearance resembling the meaning of various characteristics": this means that there arises an appearance resembling the various characteristics of the collections of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*); furthermore, it means that those [appearances] also arise resembling the various characteristics of the meanings designated by names upon which they depend.
Within this, one enters the contemplation of the three natures, which is illustrated by the analogy of a rope.
Regarding "mastery over the six kinds of objects," this refers to mastery over the six kinds of objects, namely name and so forth; "mastery" is said because they are eliminated.
The Commentary states:
Because this bodhisattva thus enters into mental verbalization that resembles objective referents, they attain entry into the nature of parikalpita (the imagined).
Because they enter into vijñapti-mātra (consciousness-only), they attain entry into the nature of paratantra (the dependent).
What is the entry into the nature of perfection?
It is when one abandons the notion of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

When that mental discourse produced by the perfuming of hearing the Dharma occurs, at that time the Bodhisattva abandons the notion of objects (*artha*), because there is no place for the appearance of any objects to arise. Consequently, even the manifestation resembling representation-only cannot arise; thus, abiding in the non-discrimination of all names and objects, one dwells in direct realization corresponding to the *dharmadhātu*.

At that time, non-conceptual wisdom arises for the Bodhisattva in which the subject (ālambaka) and the object (ālambana) are equal and identical; this is the Bodhisattva’s entry into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The commentary states:

"Because one enters into mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that resembles objects" means that since all objects are merely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one thus enters into the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Regarding "because of entering into representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*): this refers to the fact that these mental verbalizations (*manojalpa*) are subsumed under representation-only, whereby one enters into the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Regarding "there is no place for the arising of anything resembling all objects": this means that because there is no category of arising that resembles objects, the category of representation-only likewise cannot arise.
Why is this? Because when one gives rise to the discrimination of "consciousness-only," it then becomes an object (artha).

Subsequently, one realizes true suchness (tathatā); since this suchness is ineffable and can only be known internally, at that time the bodhisattva attains the equality of the grasper and the grasped.

Regarding the arising of the wisdom of equality and non-discrimination: it means that the two dharmas—the wisdom that takes as its object and the *tathatā* (suchness) which is the object—are equal in essence, like space. This refers to abiding in a state where there is no essence of either grasper or grasped; because one does not discriminate between grasper and grasped, it is called "non-discriminative," which is precisely the attainment of entry into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding the statement "dwelling within the names of all non-conceptual meanings," this refers to: what are these names?
How many varieties of these names are there?
This is demonstrated by the following verse:
The treatise says:
Herein there is a verse:
“The person, the phenomena, and the meaning of the phenomena, Whether their nature be extensive or concise,”
Impurity, purity, and their ultimate limit—these are called the distinctions of the object (*viṣaya*).
The commentary states:
therein, "phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), the eye (*cakṣus*), and so forth.
As for personal names, these refer to those such as Dharmapriya, Śraddhācārin, and Dharmacārin.
Furthermore, there are names of dharmas, which refer to the sūtras and so forth.
A "meaning-name" refers to the meaning manifested by way of the dharma.
A "general name" is, for example, the term "sentient beings.
A "particular name" refers to the individual names that each of those sentient beings possesses.
The name for "nature" refers to the root of syllables.
The name for "impurity" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and the like.
The name for "purity" refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*).
Regarding names that reach the ultimate, these refer to the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena as objects of cognition.

Furthermore, ten kinds of names are briefly explained as the objects of focus for bodhisattvas: namely, names of phenomena (*dharma-nāman*), such as "eye" and so forth; and names of persons (*pudgala-nāman*), such as "I" and so forth.
Furthermore, "name by way of phenomena" refers to the teachings of the twelve divisions of scripture;
"name by way of meaning" refers to the meanings of those very twelve divisions of scripture;
and "collective name" refers to all phenomena, such as the conditioned and the unconditioned.
"Alternative names" refers to form, sensation, and so forth, as well as space and so forth.
"Names based on nature" refers to those beginning with the letter A and ending with the letter Ha.
"Impure names" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and the like.
Regarding "purity" (*viśuddhi*), it refers to the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) and so forth.
Regarding "ultimate naming" (*nāmaparyanta*), it takes the common characteristics of phenomena (*dharmasāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

These are the objects of two types of wisdom: supramundane wisdom (*lokottarajñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*tatprṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This is because they take the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena as their object and the various characteristics of all phenomena as their object, respectively; just as, within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), these are the objects of the wisdom that universally perceives the common characteristics of all meanings.
These and other such names refer to the spheres of activity of these bodhisattvas.
The Treatise says:
Because this bodhisattva thus enters into consciousness-only, they attain entry into the characteristic of what is to be known (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*).

By entering through the characteristics of what should be known, one immediately enters the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), thoroughly penetrates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, and attains the mind of equality toward all sentient beings, the mind of equality toward all bodhisattvas, and the mind of equality toward all Buddhas.
This is precisely the bodhisattva’s attainment of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
The commentary states:
"Attaining birth in the family of the Tathāgata" means that the lineage of the Buddha is not interrupted.

One who attains the mind of equality toward all sentient beings is like one who desires to enter nirvāṇa for oneself; it is the same for all sentient beings. Because of this mind, it is called the "mind of equality toward all sentient beings."
One who attains the impartial mind of all bodhisattvas does so because they have equally attained a profound and pure mind.

One who attains the impartial mind of all buddhas does so because, while abiding in this stage, they attain the dharmakāya of all buddhas; by attaining the dharmakāya, they immediately attain the impartial mind of all buddhas.

Furthermore, regarding the mind of equality toward all sentient beings: because one attains equality between self and others, just as one desires to exhaust all suffering for oneself, one does so for them as well.
The impartial mind of all bodhisattvas refers to attaining a profound and pure mind equal to that of all other bodhisattvas, thereby performing deeds that benefit sentient beings.
Attaining the impartial mind of all Buddhas refers to seeing that the dharma-realm of all Buddhas is no different from one’s own.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, for what reason does one enter the contemplation of consciousness-only?

It is for the sake of taking the universal characteristic of phenomena as an object; for the sake of supramundane *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* wisdom; and for the sake of the subsequently attained wisdom that cognizes various characteristics.

One enters the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) in order to extinguish all causal seeds of the *ālayavijñāna* which possess the characteristics of existence; to increase and attain the seeds of the *dharmakāya*; to effect the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); to give birth to all Buddha-dharmas; and to attain the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The commentary states:
Regarding "the wisdom of śamatha and vipaśyanā," this is because śamatha and vipaśyanā themselves are designated as wisdom.

Within this context, "the extinction of all causal-sign seeds of the ālayavijñāna" refers to those that possess causal signs; these are the causal conditions, namely, all the seeds of defiled phenomena within the ālayavijñāna.
Furthermore, the term "characteristic" (*nimitta*) is used to demonstrate that these very seeds serve as the objective characteristic (*ālambana-nimitta*).
Having stated this, it is shown that both the cause and the fruit of these seeds are simultaneously extinguished.
The Commentary states:

Furthermore, regarding that subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), because one perceives all the natures and characteristics of the consciousnesses produced from the *ālayavijñāna* as being like illusions and so forth, one naturally no longer falls into error.
Therefore, just as a magician acts within his magical illusions, when a bodhisattva explains cause and effect among various phenomena, he remains unerring at all times.
The commentary states:
If non-conceptual wisdom were to eliminate obstacles and give rise to the Buddha-dharmas, what further use would there be for subsequently attained wisdom?
Non-conceptual wisdom cannot explain the dharmas of cause and effect.
Why is this? Because it is free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).

Therefore, one must rely on subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) to explain those phenomena of cause and effect; at all times, these are non-erroneous, just as a magician is with respect to his magical illusions.
"All that is produced from the ālayavijñāna" means that all these have the ālayavijñāna as their cause.
"Among all the natures and characteristics of consciousness" means that they take the nature of consciousness as their cause.
Just as with illusory phenomena, the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) speaks of them without inversion, and thus it is not erroneous.
The treatise states:
Within this entry into the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), there are four types of *samādhi* that serve as the basis for the four types of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
How is it to be perceived?
It is by means of the fourfold investigation of objects.
Through the receptivity to the absence of objects at the lower level, one attains the clear samādhi, which serves as the basis for the stage of "heat" within the aids to penetration.
If superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) further clarifies samādhi, it serves as the basis for the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), which is the part conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).
By means of four kinds of thorough knowledge (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*), one attains entry into the certainty that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) and that external objects do not exist.
This samādhi, which enters into one portion of the true meaning, is the basis for the patience that accords with the truths (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*).

This samādhi, at its final stage, eliminates the perception of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra-saṃjñā*); it is the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) samādhi, which is the basis for the "highest mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*). It should be viewed in this way.
It should be understood that these various samādhis belong to the limit of the correct position (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The commentary states:
"In all cases, upon entering into reality, one attains the stage of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*)."
Now, herein it is also shown that the basis for the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is called the "basis" because it is the cause of penetration.

Regarding the phrase "attaining the samādhi of clarity through the inferior stage of receptivity to the absence of objects": this means that within the state of the absence of objects, there is a slight degree of aspiration; the wisdom regarding the absence of objects is designated as "clarity."
"Attaining the samādhi of clarity" is stated because it reveals the samādhi that serves as the basis for non-objectifying wisdom (*nirnimitta-jñāna*).
"Supreme patience regarding the absence of objects" is mentioned because, in this context, patience is itself a form of aspiration (*chanda*).
Regarding the samādhi called "Increasing Clarity" (*vṛddhāloka*): "clarity" (*āloka*) indicates that it is named for the superior wisdom that is free from objective dust;
"samādhi" indicates that it is the basis upon which this wisdom free from objective dust relies.

Regarding that which is the basis for the patience that accords with the truths (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*): the "truth" is the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), because one possesses patience that accords with that selflessness.
How is this patience that accords with the truths established?
Because it is determined that there are no external objects distinct [from consciousness], the grasper (*grāhaka*) also does not exist.
One should know that this aspiration is attained when abiding in the swift and sharp *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformable patience).
"The limit of the correct position" (*samyaktva-nyāma*) refers to the time of the correct position itself.
The treatise says:
Thus, because a bodhisattva who has entered the stages enters into consciousness-only, they attain the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
How does one initiate the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?

In accordance with what has been established, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are taught. Taking as their object the common characteristics of all phenomena that encompass and manifest the reality present in all *sūtras*, one practices for the sake of attaining the three bodies of the Buddha by means of supramundane and subsequently attained wisdoms of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, having cultivated them for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* eons, thereby effecting the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
The commentary states:
"Speaking according to what is established" means that one speaks of the various stages within the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* for the sake of establishing them.

"Taking the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as the object-condition" means taking the single characteristic as the object-condition, rather than taking each individual phrase as a separate object-condition.
That which transcends the world refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
That which is subsequently attained refers to the wisdom of establishment (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
This, too, cannot be said to be worldly.

Why is this? Because it is not due to worldly habitual practice, nor is it exclusively supramundane, since it accords with worldly conduct; thus, it cannot be definitively described as having a single characteristic.
"To serve as the basis for transformation" means that by means of this wisdom which takes general characteristics as its object, one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
"To attain the three bodies of a Buddha" means that one practices with the thought: "May I attain the three bodies of a Buddha."
The Treatise says:
Regarding the entry into the stage of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by Śrāvakas and the entry into the stage of correctness by Bodhisattvas, what is the difference between these two?
One should know that there are ten kinds of distinctions within the Śrāvaka’s stage of correctness, which differ from the Bodhisattva’s stage of correctness.
First, the distinction of the object of focus (*ālambana*), because the Mahāyāna teachings serve as the object of focus.
Second, the distinction of maintenance (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because it is maintained by the great accumulations of merit and wisdom.
Third, the distinction of penetration (*prativedha*), because one penetrates the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
Fourth is the distinction of nirvāṇa, because it encompasses the nirvāṇa that dwells nowhere and clings to nothing.
Fifth is the distinction of the stages, because it relies on the transcendence of the ten bhūmis.
Sixth is the distinction of purity, because of the abandonment of afflictions and the purification of the Buddha-fields.
Seventh is the distinction of attaining a mind of equality between all sentient beings and oneself, because one initiates the practice of maturing sentient beings without rest.
Eighth is the distinction of birth, because one is born into the family of the Tathāgata.
Ninth is the distinction of manifestations, because it is comprised of all-time manifestations within the assembly of the Buddha’s wheel.

Tenth is the distinction of results, because it is the accomplishment of the fruits of immeasurable merits such as the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
The commentary states:
Regarding the distinction in *nirvāṇa*, it is because the bodhisattva embraces the *nirvāṇa* of non-abiding, whereas the śrāvaka does not.

Regarding the distinction in purity, it is because the bodhisattva eliminates both afflictions and their residual impressions (*vāsanā*) while purifying the buddha-fields, whereas the śrāvaka does not.
The treatise says:
Herein there is a verse:
When one investigates names and their referents, Each is merely a guest to the other.
Investigating the two as mere cognition, and likewise the two as mere designations;
