Furthermore, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) is always in association with various hosts such as devas; such association is inconsistent with the essential body (svabhāvakāya). Therefore, the enjoyment body is not identical to the essential body.

Furthermore, once the ālayavijñāna has undergone the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti), one immediately attains the svabhāvakāya. If this very svabhāvakāya were itself the saṃbhogakāya, then after the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) have undergone the transformation of the basis, what further body would be attained?
Therefore, the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) is not identical to the Nature Body (svabhāvakāya).
Because of these six kinds of inconsistencies, they cannot be one and the same.
The Treatise says:
For what reasons is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) also not the essential body (*svabhāvakāya*)?
There are eight reasons.
First, because bodhisattvas who have attained non-retrogressive samādhi since time immemorial do not manifest [as ordinary beings] when born in Tuṣita Heaven or among human beings.

Second, because one lacks wisdom regarding the knowledge of past lives, writing, calculation, arithmetic, seals, arts and crafts, various treatises, and the practice of enjoying sensual desires, [the goal] is not accomplished.
Third, because one has already understood the teachings of false doctrines and correct Dharma yet still goes to the dwellings of non-Buddhists, [the goal] is not accomplished.
Fourth, because he practiced asceticism while fully knowing the paths of the three vehicles, it would not have been accomplished.
Fifth, because he abandoned ten billion Jambudvīpas to realize perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma in a single location, it would not have been accomplished.

Sixth, if apart from such skillful means as manifesting the realization of perfect enlightenment, all other buddha-activities were performed solely through the nirmāṇakāya, then one would have to realize perfect enlightenment within the Tuṣita Heaven.
Seventh: Why is it that a Buddha does not appear simultaneously and equally throughout all Jambudvīpas?
Since this is not the case, there is neither scripture (*āgama*) nor logical reasoning (*yukti*) to prove it.
It is not contradictory for two Tathāgatas to appear in the world simultaneously within a single world-system, because there exist numerous transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*).
When it is said "one world," this refers to a single four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*), just as two universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) do not appear together.
In this regard, there is a verse:
The subtle transformations of the Buddhas, Entering equally into many wombs,
Are the perfect awakening in all its aspects, Manifesting for the sake of taking birth.
The commentary states:
Next, it is shown that the nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) is inconsistent with the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
There are eight kinds of inconsistency.

Regarding the first point among these, those bodhisattvas who have attained non-retrogressive samādhi since immeasurable kalpas in the distant past do not even take birth among the various heavens such as Tuṣita, much less among human beings.
Therefore, that which is seen in the world is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), not the *svabhāvakāya* (essential body).
Furthermore, it would be illogical for bodhisattvas who have already attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) to be ignorant of matters such as writing and arithmetic.
Therefore, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) performs these deeds in order to teach and transform sentient beings.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they do not yet know the difference between right teaching and false teaching; how then could they know it upon attaining perfect enlightenment at the final stage?
Therefore, the transformation body is not the essential body.
Furthermore, it would be illogical for one to abandon ten billion Jambudvīpas and realize perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma in only a single location.
If the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) were established [as the ultimate reality], it would manifest simultaneously in all places; therefore, the emanation body is not the essential body (svabhāvakāya).

If you claim that one attains perfect enlightenment in only one place while manifesting the emanation body along with its retinue in other locations, why does one not attain perfect enlightenment while remaining in Tuṣita Heaven itself, rather than manifesting the emanation body throughout all four continents?

If it is claimed that one does not realize perfect enlightenment within any of the four continents among all the four-continent worlds, this argument is untenable, as there is neither scriptural authority (*āgama*) nor logical reasoning (*yukti*) to prove that one does not realize perfect enlightenment within any particular four-continent world within a single Buddha-field.
If you say that this contradicts the sūtras, why is that?
It should be understood that the sūtras state that two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously.
The analogy of the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) mentioned in that sutra refers to the fact that two wheel-turning monarchs do not appear simultaneously;
this means they do not appear concurrently within a single four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*), not within a single buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*).
The same applies to the fact that two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously. As for what is called a "world," it refers to a single four-continent system (*cāturdvīpaka*).
Within this context, there is a verse that illustrates perfect awakening; its meaning is precisely the subtle transformations and other such qualities of the Buddhas.

When the Buddha was dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, if he descended into the womb, one should know that at that time, any who were present with him as his retinue—such as the Elder Śāriputra and others—were all merely manifestations established through transformation.
Having established it in this way, one then demonstrates the realization of perfect enlightenment within all phenomena.
The treatise says:

For the sake of all sentient beings, to aspire and practice toward the attainment of great enlightenment, yet to enter ultimate nirvana, is not logical; for such aspiration and practice would then be without fruit.
Because of this fault.
The commentary states:
This demonstrates here that ultimate nirvāṇa would not be established.

For the sake of all sentient beings, the Buddhas have made great vows and engaged in spiritual practice; having thus formed the intention to benefit all beings, they carry out whatever actions will bring them benefit according to the needs of those beings.
If one were to enter parinirvāṇa within ultimate nirvāṇa, then those vows and practices would be fruitless.
If you say that the Tathāgata’s dharma-body is eternally abiding, yet the enjoyment body and transformation body are impermanent, how can they be called an eternal body?
Now, in order to establish this point, the treatise says:
"The Enjoyment Body and the Transformation Body are both impermanent; how then can it be said that the Tathāgata’s body is eternally abiding?"

Because the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding, the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*—these two bodies—do not abandon the maturation of their retribution and repeatedly manifest transformations; thus, they enjoy bliss as if constantly and bestow food as if constantly. One should understand that the Buddha-body is eternally abiding in this manner.
The commentary states:
The two bodies are eternal because they rely upon the eternally abiding Dharma-body; thus, these two bodies are eternal.
Furthermore, as for the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), it is eternal because it does not relinquish its enjoyment.
The nirmāṇakāya is eternal because it constantly manifests the uninterrupted succession of such signs as the attainment of perfect enlightenment and parinirvāṇa;
thus, its eternity is demonstrated through these two bodies by means of analogies.
It is like the worldly expression "constantly experiencing pleasure," which does not mean that one obtains uninterrupted pleasure to be called "constantly experiencing pleasure.

Or again, it is like saying "this person constantly gives food," which does not mean they give food at all times—since there are times when they do not give—it is nevertheless called "one who constantly gives food."
The meaning of the permanence of the two bodies is likewise.
The treatise says:
Due to six causes and conditions, the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not abide eternally.
First, the completion of what is to be done, meaning that sentient beings have already been brought to maturity and liberation.
Second, the turning away from the desire for nirvāṇa, causing them to seek the eternally abiding Buddha-body.
Third, it is to cultivate the intention for practice directed toward the Buddha, so as to give rise to clear understanding within the correct exposition of the profound Dharma.
Fourth, it is to generate a sense of longing and veneration, for even frequent sight of him does not lead to satiety.
Fifth is the generation of one's own diligence, because it is known that no speaker can be found.
Sixth is the attainment of extremely rapid maturation, because one initiates personal diligence and does not abandon the heavy yoke.
In this regard, there is a verse:
"The tasks to be accomplished are brought to completion;
That desire for quiescence is transformed, And the slight regard for the Buddha is turned away, Causing a heart of yearning and longing to arise."
To inspire self-initiated diligence and cause [beings] to reach swift maturation, the Buddha manifests transformation bodies; these do not abide eternally.
Although the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is beginningless and immeasurable, one should nevertheless exert diligent effort in order to attain it.
In this regard, there is a verse:
The Buddhas attain [enlightenment] through causes that are undifferentiated and immeasurable; yet sentient beings abandon diligence toward these.
If they were to attain everything [merely by wishing], it would follow that nothing is cause and effect; such a severance of causality is illogical.
The explanation of the "Mahāyānasaṃgraha" chapter within the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra* is completed.
Composed by the Ācārya Asaṅga.
The commentary states:
In this regard, there is an objection:
If the Dharmakāya is without beginning, undifferentiated, and limitless, and for this reason is capable of benefiting sentient beings, why is it necessary to exert diligent effort for its sake?
To refute that objection, it is demonstrated by verse:
"The qualities attained by those Buddhas are non-different and immeasurable; taking this as the cause, one should arouse right diligence."
Therefore, to say that the Buddhas have no beginning entails all manner of faults.
Why is this? Because it results in the logical fallacy of a cause that cannot be established at any time.
Such a refutation of the cause is unreasonable.

For all Bodhisattvas, great compassion dwells in their hearts; they cherish all sentient beings as if they were their only child. Regarding the work of benefiting sentient beings, it would be illogical to say that others act on their behalf while this is not what they themselves have undertaken.
Whatever others have done or left undone, I have performed it all; thus should it be.
This concludes the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, composed by the Ācārya Vasubandhu, who established and expounded immeasurable superior treatises within the Mahāyāna school.
